synopsis: Virtual validation must support tuning automatic-braking thresholds before field tests; SIL can exercise decision logic at scale, and object-list replay can test thresholds and brake requests independently of sensor modality [f29, f925, f528, f5256]. Simulation-tuned thresholds have been checked against field results on-road, but no published quantitative off-road comparison was found, leaving transfer to off-road operation unknown [f153, f6374, f6558]. A fixed time-to-collision threshold is considered a weak primary trigger at work-site speeds: the booklet favors distance and risk zones, while ISO 21815-3:2023 leaves machine-specific numbers to manufacturers and integrators, and neither generally tuned off-road TTC/deceleration values nor a reliable cross-product terrain-friction table was found [f13894, f6203, f5916, f6017]. Threshold selection must balance misses against nuisance interventions and task constraints; existing fleet false-alarm history is identified as the best available calibration evidence, but how warning-system tuning should carry over to automatic braking was not examined [f11305, f6569, f11519, f1168, f1170]. Tuning variables include confidence, speed-dependent zones, N-of-M track confirmation, persistence, debounce and filter constants; DOE with response surfaces suits a handful of continuous settings, whereas ROC/DET/precision-recall selection addresses only the detector threshold, not closed-loop timing and braking [f6957, f7297, f12851]. Validation must cover configurable parameters and integrator changes: modifying a threshold after inspecting audit failures contaminates the audit set, safety-relevant late threshold changes require fresh independent statistical confirmation, and ISO 16001 allows at most 300 ms detection time with an uninterrupted signal sequence [f2927, f6952, f7389, f13914].

relations.note: Both describe SIL coverage of thresholds, software logic, state transitions and regression at scale.
Both describe modality-independent threshold and brake-request testing through semantic or object-list replay.
Both identify recorded warning-fleet false alarms as the best available intervention-threshold data.
Both reject universal close-object alarming and aggressive suppression across production tasks.
Both report no published off-road comparison of simulation-tuned thresholds with field results.
Both report the missing reliable terrain-friction table for setting braking thresholds.
Both report no evidence requiring detailed terrain models coupled with multibody machines.
Glossary restates the absence of evidence requiring DEM, SPH or FEM threshold prediction.
Both report no evidence that detailed terrain modeling is required for threshold prediction.
Both say required performance level drives architecture and validation as much as threshold tuning.
Both recommend DOE and response surfaces for a small set of continuous tuning parameters.
Both limit ROC, DET and precision-recall operating-point tuning to the detector threshold.
Glossary adds distance-and-zone alternatives and retained TTC uses to the weak-trigger finding.
Hidden sensor, operator and machine uncertainties explain the weakness of a fixed TTC trigger.
Glossary explains that detector-only tuning omits closed-loop timing, braking and multiple objectives.
Missing quantitative off-road field comparisons underpin uncertainty about simulation-to-field threshold transfer.
Audit-set leakage explains why changed safety thresholds need new independent confirmation.
Obstacle-only testing biases intervention aggressively, reinforcing the need for false-alarm evidence.
